Finding Balance Counseling is the practice of Reem Glasco, LPC-S, in Cedar Park, Texas. Reem has held Texas LPC supervisor status since 2009 and is an EMDRIA Approved Consultant, a NARM therapist and a Somatic Experiencing Practitioner. She supervises LPC Associates online statewide at $425 a month, consults on EMDR at $185 an hour, and runs mindful trail and equine retreats for therapists. Clients seeking therapy are seen by Reem or by the practice's associates.

Hi, I am Reem

I have been supervising since 2009, and the associates I work best with want more than signed hours. They want to understand what is happening in the room, including what is happening in their own nervous system while a client is falling apart in front of them.

My clinical center is IFS-informed EMDR: processing that consults the protective parts of a person instead of overriding them. Somatic Experiencing sets the pace, NARM tracks the patterns underneath. That is what I teach, and it is what I practice.

I expect you to show up prepared, be honest, and tell me when something goes wrong. In return you get help building a practice, not just a log.

Something to try before we ever meet

Longer out-breaths than in-breaths tell a nervous system it is allowed to stand down. One minute is enough to feel the difference, which is also the argument for teaching it to clients before you teach them anything else.

If the circle distracts you, ignore it and count: in for four, hold for two, out for six.

Why four individual plus one group: Texas requires at least four hours of supervision a month and caps group supervision at half your total hours. Four and one is five hours, which clears the floor by a full hour and keeps group at a fifth, so a missed week does not put you under. The rules are laid out in full in the licensure guide.

Note for the site build: confirm the structure with Reem. The old site said four individual plus one group in one place and three plus one in another; this build uses four plus one throughout, which is five hours a month. If it is really four hours in total, the fee framing and the margin argument above both need rewording.

What supervision here is like

Supervision is not a compliance meeting. It is the place you bring the session that went sideways, the client you think about on the drive home, and the parts of the work that are touching something of your own.

I work collaboratively, which means I expect you to show up prepared, be honest, and tell me when something goes wrong. In return you get someone who will help you build a practice, not just log hours: fee setting, caseload shape, online presence, referral relationships, and the ethics of all of it.

The clinical lens is trauma-informed and body-oriented. We will talk about the nervous system in the room, yours as much as the client's, and about transference and countertransference as information rather than error.

You will probably fit well here if

  • You want developmental trauma and C-PTSD work to be a real part of your training.
  • You are drawn to NARM, Somatic Experiencing, EMDR, IFS-informed work or Brainspotting.
  • You intend to build a private practice, now or eventually.
  • You can tolerate direct feedback and want it.
  • You are curious about experiential and body-based supervision, including work with horses.

LPC supervision questions

How much does LPC supervision cost in Texas with Reem Glasco?

Supervision is $425 a month, which covers four individual supervision hours and one group hour. Associates working inside an agency or group practice can arrange a three-month contract at $500 a month. Optional equine-assisted sessions are $60 each.

How many supervision hours do I get each month?

Five: four individual hours and one group hour, based on a caseload of ten or more clients a week. If your caseload or board requirements differ, raise it in the consult and we will plan the cadence together.

Is supervision online or in person?

Supervision is online only, which means any LPC Associate licensed in Texas can work with Reem regardless of where in the state they live. The optional equine sessions and the annual retreat are the in-person exceptions.

Are there supervision openings right now?

One spot opens in fall 2026 and one in spring 2027. Because supervision is capped deliberately, it is worth booking a consult before a spot opens rather than after.

Do you provide a placement site for supervisees?

Yes, online only. Site verification is part of the application process, so the placement details are confirmed before any agreement is signed.

Does supervision include EMDR consultation?

Yes. Reem is an EMDRIA Approved Consultant and offers free individual EMDR consults to her own associates. Paid consultation toward EMDR certification is available separately to therapists who are not supervisees.

What does Reem expect from a supervisee?

Show up prepared, be honest, and communicate when something goes wrong. Supervision works when the hard material arrives in the room rather than getting managed outside it.

What is equine-assisted supervision?

Optional in-person sessions with horses near Dripping Springs, Texas, at $60 each. Horses respond to what your nervous system is doing rather than what you intend, which makes them an unusually direct teacher of presence and of your own countertransference. Training for therapists working with horses is also available for an additional fee.

Consultation questions

Do these hours count toward EMDR certification?

Reem is an EMDRIA Approved Consultant, which is the credential EMDRIA requires for consultation hours toward certification. Confirm your own current requirements with EMDRIA, since their criteria are set by them and can change.

How much does EMDR consultation cost?

$185 for an individual online hour. LPC Associates under Reem's supervision receive individual EMDR consults at no additional cost.

I am not in Texas. Can we still work together?

Consultation is a peer professional relationship rather than clinical care, so it is not limited to Texas in the way therapy and LPC supervision are. Check what your own licensing board expects of your consultation arrangements.

What if my EMDR training was years ago?

That is common and it is a fine place to start. Bring a case you feel stuck on and we will rebuild confidence from the preparation phases forward rather than starting from the manual.

Also worth knowing

If you are an LPC Associate rather than a licensed therapist, EMDR consultation comes free with supervision here. And if you are still working out the Texas requirements, the licensure guide has the numbers.

Why any of this, when you already have supervision

Because the thing that limits most clinicians is not knowledge. It is how much they can stay present for before something in them takes over: the urge to fix, to reassure, to change the subject, to work harder than the client.

That capacity does not grow much by talking about it. It grows by being in a situation where your own state is the material, and then noticing what you do. Walking does some of that. Horses do a lot of it.

Reem and Blu, near Dripping Springs.

Mindful trail retreats

An annual retreat for interns, associates and licensed therapists. We walk, and the subject is presence: what it feels like when you have it, what takes it away, and what you do instead when you have lost it.

It is not a conference and there is no curriculum to get through. Expect quiet, movement, small-group work, and more silence than most professional events are comfortable with.

Associates in supervision with Reem are included in the annual retreat. Others are welcome as space allows.

Good fit if

  • You give your clients regulation skills you do not practice yourself.
  • You are competent and quietly exhausted.
  • You want professional development that is not another slide deck.
  • You are curious about somatic work but have only read about it.

Working with horses

Horses respond to what your nervous system is doing, not to what you intend or say. A therapist who is subtly braced gets a different horse than one who is settled, and the feedback arrives in seconds rather than in a supervision session three weeks later.

Two ways in. Associates in supervision can add equine-assisted sessions at $60 each as part of their supervision. Licensed therapists who want to bring horses into their own practice can train with Reem, for a separate fee.

Ethics CEUs for Texas LPCs

Texas LPCs need 24 continuing education hours in each two-year renewal period, including at least 6 hours in ethics, and since January 2024 at least half of the total must come from a provider listed in §681.140(f). Reem offers ethics continuing education periodically.

The full renewal requirements are in the licensure guide, including what LPC-S status adds.

Note for the site build: list the next retreat date, the equine training format and fee, and the next ethics CEU offering with its provider approval, then link a registration route. Until those are set, this page sends people to the contact form.

Questions

Do I have to be Reem's supervisee to attend a retreat?

No. Associates in supervision with Reem are included, and other interns, associates and licensed therapists are welcome as space allows.

How much do the equine sessions cost?

$60 per session for LPC Associates in supervision with Reem, added on to the $425 monthly supervision fee. Training for therapists who want to work with horses in their own practice is priced separately per offering.

Do the ethics CEUs count toward Texas LPC renewal?

Ethics hours count toward the 6-hour ethics requirement inside your 24 hours per renewal period. Because at least half your total hours must come from a provider listed in 22 TAC §681.140(f), always confirm the provider status of any offering, including this one, before you rely on it.

Is any of this therapy?

No. Retreats and training are professional development, and supervision is supervision. If what you need is your own therapy, that is a good thing to want, and Reem can point you to a referral rather than mixing the roles.

Continuing education for Texas counselors

Ethics CEUs

Texas LPCs need 24 hours of continuing education each renewal period, at least 6 of them in ethics. Reem Glasco, LPC-S, offers ethics continuing education in two formats: one CEU online, or two CEUs in person, held on a trail walk among horses near Dripping Springs. The subject is secondary trauma: what this work does to the people who do it, and where the ethical obligations actually sit.

Email about the next session The CE requirements in full

The two formats

Both count as ethics hours. The in-person session is the one that is hard to find anywhere else.
FormatCEUsWhereSubject
Online 1 ethics CEU Zoom, anywhere Secondary trauma
In person, on a trail walk among horses 2 ethics CEUs Near Dripping Springs, Texas Secondary trauma

Note for the site build: add the next dates, the fee and the §681.140(f) approved provider status, then replace the email button with a registration route. Until the provider status is stated, a prospective attendee cannot tell whether these hours count toward their required half, which is the first thing a careful LPC checks.

Why secondary trauma, for an ethics hour

Ethics continuing education is often taught as a tour of the rules: boundaries, record keeping, dual relationships, the things you already know and will be reminded of once every two years. That version is survivable and forgettable.

Secondary trauma gets at the part of ethics that actually goes wrong in practice. Competence is an ethical obligation, and competence degrades when a clinician is depleted in ways they have stopped noticing. Most ethical failures in this field are not decisions made badly; they are attention that was no longer there.

So the session looks at what accumulates across a caseload, how it shows up before you can name it, what the obligation to monitor your own fitness to practice means concretely, and when it requires you to do something about it.

Walking it, rather than sitting through it

The two-CEU version is held outdoors, walking, among horses. That is not a gimmick attached to the content; it is the content. A room full of therapists discussing depletion while sitting still for two hours is its own small joke. Walking changes what people say, and horses respond to the state of the person in front of them rather than the credential.

It also means you leave having practiced the thing rather than having heard about it.

Who it is for

  • Texas LPCs filling the 6 required ethics hours per renewal period
  • LPC Associates, who need the same hours
  • Clinicians who suspect they are running on empty and would rather find out on purpose

Questions about the CEUs

How many ethics CEUs do Texas LPCs need?

At least 6 hours of ethics within the 24 hours of continuing education required each renewal period. Passing the jurisprudence exam counts as one of those ethics hours. LPC Supervisors need a further 6 hours of supervision-specific CE, counted inside the same 24.

Do these hours count toward the approved-provider half?

Since 1 January 2024 at least half of your 24 hours must come from a provider listed in 22 TAC §681.140(f). Confirm the provider status of any CE before you book it, including this one, because hours from an unlisted provider are still worth taking but do not fill that half.

What does the trail walk session involve physically?

Walking at conversation pace on a trail, with time standing among horses. It is not strenuous and there is no riding, but it is outdoors in central Texas, so it is weather dependent and gets rescheduled rather than pushed through.

Can LPC Associates attend?

Yes. Associates carry the same continuing education requirements as fully licensed LPCs and are welcome at both formats. Associates supervised by Reem are included in the annual retreat as part of their supervision.

How do I register?

Email reemglasco@gmail.com and ask about the next session. Dates and fees are not yet published here, so email is currently the only route.

Getting licensed as an LPC in Texas

Full LPC licensure in Texas requires a qualifying graduate degree, two exams, an LPC Associate license, and then 3,000 clock-hours of supervised experience under a Council-approved supervisor. At least 1,500 of those hours must be direct client counseling contact, and the 3,000 cannot be completed in fewer than 18 months. While you are accruing them you must receive at least four hours of supervision a month, with no more than half of your total supervision hours in a group. Your LPC Associate license expires 60 months from issuance and cannot be renewed.

Rules cited below are from 22 Texas Administrative Code, Chapter 681, administered by the Texas Behavioral Health Executive Council. Current as of September 2026. Rules change, so verify anything you are about to rely on against BHEC directly.

The path, in four stages

Each stage has to be complete before the next one counts.
StageWhat it takesRule
Graduate degree 60 semester hours for programs begun on or after 1 August 2017, 48 before that, including a supervised practicum of at least 300 clock-hours with at least 100 hours of direct client counseling, carrying academic credit §681.82, §681.83
Exams The NCE or the NCMHCE, plus the Texas Jurisprudence Exam. Your jurisprudence certificate must be dated no more than six months before your application is received §681.72
LPC Associate license Apply and be licensed before you begin. Hours worked while unlicensed do not count, in any setting. The license expires 60 months from issuance and cannot be renewed §681.72, §681.140
Supervised experience 3,000 clock-hours, at least 1,500 of them direct client counseling contact, over no fewer than 18 months, under a Council-approved supervisor §681.92

The hours, and how long they actually take

The 3,000 is rarely the binding constraint. The 1,500 direct hours are, because direct hours accrue only while you are in session with a client. Everything else, notes, admin, training, staffing, counts toward the other 1,500.

Time to reach 1,500 direct hours, before holidays, no-shows and ramp-up.
Direct client hours a weekWeeks to 1,500Roughly
256018 months, held to the floor
207518 months, held to the floor
151002 years
121252 years 5 months
81883 years 7 months

Two things fall out of that table. Above roughly twenty direct hours a week, the 18-month floor decides your timeline, not your caseload, so pushing harder buys you nothing. Below about twelve, the 60-month expiry on your Associate license starts to become the real deadline, and cancellations and slow referral months eat the margin faster than most associates expect.

The supervision rules associates get wrong

  • Four hours a month is a minimum, not a target. You must receive at least four hours of supervision in every month you are counseling, unless your supervisor approves an extended leave of a month or more in writing.
  • Individual means up to two associates. BHEC defines individual supervision as a supervisor with one or two associates. Three or more is group.
  • No more than half your total hours can be group. Over the whole period, group supervision cannot exceed 50% of your supervision hours. This is why a structure of four individual hours plus one group hour a month works cleanly: group is a fifth of the total.
  • Two supervisors, maximum. You may have up to two LPC supervisors on file at a time, splitting hours by mutual agreement.
  • Paperwork has deadlines. The Supervisory Agreement Form goes in before supervision starts. The Supervised Experience Documentation Form is due within 30 days after supervision ends.
  • Miss the 60 months and you start over. If the required hours are not complete when your Associate license expires, you reapply and meet whatever requirements are in effect at that time.

How supervision with Reem is structured

Choosing a supervisor

You will spend eighteen months to three years with this person, during the period that shapes how you practice for the rest of your career. Interview them.

Worth asking

  • How many associates are you supervising right now, and what is your cap?
  • What is the fee, what does it include, and does it change if my caseload changes?
  • Is the fee monthly or hourly, and what happens in a month when I only need two hours?
  • How is group supervision structured, and how many people are in it?
  • Are you reachable between sessions when something urgent comes up?
  • What are your clinical models, and are you willing to supervise work outside them?
  • Will you help me build a practice, or only sign hours?
  • How do you give corrective feedback, and can you give me an example?
  • Who employs me, and does that create a conflict with who supervises me?

Reasons to walk away

  • No written supervision agreement.
  • The Supervisory Agreement Form is not filed before you start seeing clients.
  • Hours are not documented contemporaneously, or records are treated as the supervisor's property.
  • Sessions get canceled and not rescheduled, leaving you short for the month.
  • You cannot get a straight answer about fees.
  • Feedback is only reassurance. If nothing you do is ever questioned, you are paying for a signature.

What supervision costs

Fee structures vary more than the headline number suggests. Some supervisors charge per hour, some charge a flat monthly rate covering the full four hours, and some charge less per hour but exclude group. Agencies sometimes cover supervision entirely, sometimes in exchange for a lower fee split, which is a real cost even when it is not an invoice.

Compare on the monthly total for four compliant hours, not on the hourly rate. Then ask what else is included: EMDR or modality consultation, practice-building help, a placement site, retreats, access between sessions.

For reference, supervision with Reem is $425 a month covering four individual hours and one group hour, or $500 a month on a three-month contract for associates inside an agency. EMDR consultation is included at no cost while you are her associate.

Renewing your Texas LPC license

Renewal is where most licensed counselors interact with the rules, and it is separate from everything above: the 3,000 hours get you licensed once, the renewal cycle keeps you licensed for the rest of your career. What BHEC requires each renewal period is continuing education, the jurisprudence exam, and the fee.

Continuing education
24 hours in each renewal period
Ethics inside that 24
At least 6 hours
Cultural diversity and competency
At least 3 hours, inside the 24
Approved providers
Since 1 January 2024, at least half of the 24 hours must come from a provider listed in §681.140(f)
Human trafficking prevention
An HHSC-approved course
Jurisprudence exam
Passed each renewal period, and it counts as one hour of ethics credit
LPC Supervisors
A further 6 hours of supervision-specific continuing education per renewal period, counted inside the 24
Fees, dates and late renewal
Set by BHEC and not reproduced here. Check your renewal notice and the BHEC renewal page before your expiry date.

Two things catch people out. The first is the approved-provider rule: hours from an unlisted provider still count toward professional development but not toward your required half, so check the provider before you pay, not after. The second is that supervision CE for an LPC-S is not additional to the 24, it sits inside it, which means a supervisor has less free choice about the other hours than they might assume.

This page does not list renewal fees or late-renewal windows, because those are set by BHEC and change more often than the rule text does. Take them from your renewal notice or from BHEC directly rather than from any third-party site, this one included.

Ethics CEUs and training with Reem

Becoming a supervisor

Becoming an LPC-S

Supervisor status requires an unrestricted LPC license in good standing for at least five years, plus either a 40-clock-hour supervision course meeting §681.147 or a for-credit doctoral-level course in supervision. Once approved, holding it requires 6 hours of supervision-specific continuing education per renewal period, which count inside the 24.

BHEC's current guidance says the supervision course does not expire once completed, while the rule text has historically referenced recency windows. If your certificate is old, confirm with BHEC before you apply.

What it lets you do

An approved LPC-S can supervise LPC Associates toward their own 3,000 hours, which is the arrangement this whole guide describes from the other side. It is also the credential that makes a practice's supervision revenue possible, which is why the five-year unrestricted-license requirement exists.

Supervisory status is maintained on the same renewal cycle as the license itself, with the 6 supervision CE hours counted inside the 24.

Supervision with Reem, an LPC-S since 2009

Texas LPC licensure questions

How many supervised hours do you need for an LPC in Texas?

3,000 clock-hours of supervised experience under a Council-approved supervisor, of which at least 1,500 must be direct client counseling contact. Only actual time spent counseling counts as direct. The 3,000 cannot be completed in fewer than 18 months, per 22 TAC §681.92.

How many hours of supervision does an LPC Associate need each month?

A minimum of four hours a month while you are counseling. Individual supervision means a supervisor with one or two associates; group means three or more. No more than 50% of your total supervision hours may be group. You can have up to two LPC supervisors on file at once.

How long does it take to become an LPC in Texas?

Eighteen months at the absolute fastest after you are licensed as an Associate, because that floor applies regardless of how quickly you accrue hours. At fifteen direct client hours a week it takes about two years; at eight a week, closer to three and a half. Add the two to three years of graduate study before that.

Does my LPC Associate license expire?

Yes. It expires 60 months from the date of issuance and cannot be renewed. If you have not completed the required supervised experience in that window, you must reapply for licensure and meet the requirements in effect at the time of reapplication.

Do hours count if I worked before getting my Associate license?

No. Hours obtained by an unlicensed person do not count toward the supervised experience requirement, in any setting. Get licensed first.

Can I do supervision online in Texas?

Yes. Texas rules set the amount and structure of supervision rather than requiring it to be in person, and online supervision is common across the state. Reem Glasco, LPC-S, supervises online only, which means associates anywhere in Texas can work with her.

What qualifies someone to supervise LPC Associates in Texas?

An unrestricted Texas LPC license in good standing for at least five years, plus a 40-clock-hour supervision course meeting 22 TAC §681.147 or a for-credit doctoral-level course in supervision, and approval by BHEC as an LPC-S. Verify any supervisor's status on the BHEC license lookup before signing an agreement.

What do you need to renew a Texas LPC license?

24 hours of continuing education in each renewal period, including at least 6 hours of ethics and 3 hours of cultural diversity and competency, an HHSC-approved human trafficking prevention course, and a pass on the jurisprudence exam, which itself counts as one hour of ethics credit. Since 1 January 2024, at least half of the 24 hours must come from a provider listed in 22 TAC §681.140(f). Fees and dates come from BHEC.

How many CE hours does a Texas LPC Supervisor need?

The same 24 as any LPC, with 6 of them in supervision-specific continuing education to maintain supervisory status. Those 6 sit inside the 24 rather than on top of it, so an LPC-S has fewer discretionary hours than a licensee without the credential.

Do continuing education hours from any provider count?

Not toward the whole requirement. Since 1 January 2024 at least half of the 24 hours must come from a provider listed in §681.140(f). Hours from an unlisted provider can still be worth taking, but they do not fill that half, so confirm the provider's status before booking rather than after.

What trauma work looks like here

Nothing gets opened faster than you can stay present for. That is not caution for its own sake: a nervous system that floods learns that attention to the body is dangerous, and then the work gets harder rather than easier.

You do not have to tell the whole story. Somatic Experiencing tracks what the body is still holding rather than what the mind can narrate, and NARM asks where a pattern was learned and whether it is still serving you, rather than excavating the past for its own sake.

With developmental trauma we are usually building capacity rather than processing a single event, so the arc is longer and the review is done together instead of guessed at the start.

What people bring here

  • Patterns that formed early, before there were words or choices for them.
  • C-PTSD and PTSD, including trauma that has not finished happening.
  • Understanding your history perfectly well and nothing changing.
  • Going numb, or flooding, whenever you approach the hard material.
  • Self-criticism doing most of the talking.

If EMDR has stalled before

Standard EMDR asks you to hold a memory and let the processing run. For developmental trauma that instruction often meets an internal objection: a part of you that has spent years keeping the material at a distance, and has good reasons.

IFS-informed EMDR treats that objection as information rather than resistance. We get to know the protector, find out what it needs in place first, and start processing when the protective parts agree to it rather than when the protocol says it is time. Reem's emphasis is phases one and two, preparation and history-taking, because that is where stalled EMDR actually stalls.

Questions about trauma therapy

What is developmental trauma, and how is it different from PTSD?

PTSD usually refers to the aftermath of an identifiable event. Developmental trauma is what accumulates from the ongoing conditions of early life: attunement that was not there, needs that were not safe to have, adaptations that worked then and cost you now. There is often no single memory to point at, which is why event-focused protocols alone can miss it.

Do I have to tell you everything that happened?

No. Somatic Experiencing and NARM both work with what is present now rather than requiring a full retelling, and EMDR processing does not need a narrated account either. You decide what gets said out loud and when.

How long does trauma therapy take?

It depends what we are working with. Stabilization can be a handful of sessions. Developmental trauma is slower, because we are building capacity rather than processing a single event. We review the arc together rather than guessing at the start.

I have tried EMDR before and it stalled. What is different here?

Most stalled EMDR stalls in preparation rather than processing. The IFS-informed approach looks for the part of you that is objecting, works out what it needs in place first, and only then returns to the target. Reem is an EMDRIA Approved Consultant who consults with other therapists on exactly this problem.

Do you work with trauma that is still happening?

Yes. Ongoing stress and unfinished situations are common here, and the emphasis in those cases is stabilization and footing first. Processing work before there is footing tends to destabilize rather than help.

Can I see an associate instead?

Yes, and often sooner. The practice's LPC Associates work under Reem's supervision, so the clinical lineage is the same, at lower fees including sliding scale. Say what is going on in the consult and you will be pointed at the right fit.

Anxiety as a nervous system state

Anxiety is easier to understand as a threat response that never got to finish than as a thinking error. That is why insight so often fails to help: you can know the fear is disproportionate and still have a chest that will not unclench.

Somatic Experiencing works in doses, tracking sensation and the small movements the body did not complete, which widens your window of tolerance rather than talking you out of the feeling. NARM asks where the pattern was learned and what it was protecting. When specific memories or triggers are reliably hijacking you, EMDR gets added.

Where anxiety sits on top of developmental trauma, which is common, the work looks like the trauma page rather than symptom management.

What people bring here

  • A body braced at rest, with nothing in particular happening.
  • Panic attacks, and then anxiety about the next panic attack.
  • Social anxiety: rehearsing conversations before and reviewing them after.
  • Anxiety that lives in the chest and stomach more than in the thoughts.
  • Sleep that will not arrive, or arrives and does not restore.
  • Coping that works well enough at work and collapses at home.

Social anxiety specifically

Social anxiety is usually relational in origin, so it responds to relational work. NARM's question is not how to perform better in the room but what you learned about being seen, and what it cost to be yourself in front of other people.

The pacing matters more than usual here. Being asked to push into exposure before your system has any footing tends to confirm the fear rather than disprove it.

Questions about anxiety therapy

Do you treat panic attacks?

Yes. Panic is usually treated as a nervous system event rather than a thought to correct: what the system was bracing for, what the response never completed, and how to build tolerance in doses so the next wave is survivable rather than catastrophic.

Is social anxiety treated differently from general anxiety?

The lens shifts. Social anxiety is usually relational in origin, so NARM's questions about being seen and what it cost to be yourself in front of others do more work than symptom management. The old social anxiety counseling page on the previous site is now covered here.

Do you do exposure work?

Not as the main method. The Somatic Experiencing approach is titrated, meaning small doses at a pace your system can integrate, because a system that gets flooded learns that attention to itself is dangerous. Capacity comes first, contact with the feared thing after.

Do I need medication for anxiety?

That is a question for a prescriber. Reem is a Licensed Professional Counselor Supervisor, not a physician, and does not prescribe or advise on medication. Therapy and medication are not alternatives to each other, and plenty of people do both.

Does anxiety therapy work online?

Yes, and it is the default here. Body-based work translates well to video because it tracks your sensation rather than the room. Being in your own space is an advantage for some anxious systems and a distraction for others, which is worth raising in the consult.

How soon does anxiety ease?

Stabilization work often shifts something within a handful of sessions. Anxiety that sits on developmental trauma takes longer, because the target is capacity rather than a symptom. We review it together instead of promising a number at the start.

Depression as an adaptation, not a defect

Flatness is often what is left after a system has spent years managing something it could not change. Shutting down was the available option once, and it worked. NARM starts from that question rather than from diagnosis: where did I learn this, how was it serving me, is it still?

That matters because the usual instruction, try harder and do more, lands on the part of you that already believes the problem is a lack of effort. Self-criticism is not the cure for depression; it is frequently one of its engines.

Where the flatness sits on top of developmental trauma, the work looks like the trauma page. Where it alternates with a body that will not settle, see anxiety.

What people bring here

  • Flatness rather than sadness, and guilt about not being sadder.
  • Doing the things and feeling nothing about any of them.
  • Procrastination that is not laziness and does not respond to discipline.
  • A sense that something is off that you cannot point at.
  • Functioning well in public and collapsing in private.
  • Life transitions that took the floor out: graduating, leaving, arriving, becoming a parent, losing someone.
  • Self care for mothers, which usually starts with permission.

On procrastination

Procrastination that survives every productivity system is rarely about time management. More often a part of you is holding the brake for a reason, and the reason is worth knowing before it gets overridden. IFS-informed work gets to know the protector rather than pushing past it.

Pacing

Stabilization comes first: acute stress, ongoing stress, feeling overwhelmed, loss. Only with that footing does processing work become useful rather than destabilizing.

Questions about depression therapy

What if I feel nothing rather than sad?

Numbness is one of the more common presentations here and it is worth taking as seriously as sadness. It usually means a system turned the volume down on everything to survive something, and the work is restoring range rather than chasing a mood.

Is this depression or burnout?

The distinction matters less than what maintains it. Both tend to involve a nervous system that has been running on override for a long time. What we look at is what the shutdown is protecting and what would have to be true for it to relax.

Do you work with procrastination?

Yes, and specifically the kind that has outlasted every system you have tried. The working assumption is that a part of you is holding the brake for a reason worth knowing, rather than that you need better discipline.

Do I need antidepressants?

That is a question for a prescriber. Reem is a Licensed Professional Counselor Supervisor, not a physician, and does not prescribe or advise on medication. Therapy and medication are not alternatives to each other, and plenty of people do both.

I have been in therapy before and it did not help. Why would this be different?

It might not be, and that is worth saying in the consult. What is different here is the lens: body-based and developmental rather than insight-led, on the view that understanding your history and changing nothing is a common and frustrating place to get stuck.

What if I am thinking about ending my life?

This practice does not provide emergency or crisis care. Call 911 if you are in immediate danger, or call or text 988 for the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline. Once you are safe, a consult here can be a next step rather than the first one.

Why outside, and why side by side

Sitting face to face is a particular kind of pressure. Walking removes it. You are looking ahead rather than at someone looking at you, the pace gives the conversation somewhere to go, and the body is doing something while the hard material is in the air.

That suits the work here, which is body-based to begin with. Somatic Experiencing tracks sensation and the movements a threat response never finished, and movement is not a metaphor in that frame. Walking is also an easier place for some people to say a thing out loud for the first time.

It tends to suit

  • People who talk more easily in motion than in a chair.
  • Anxiety that sits in the body and settles with movement.
  • Flatness and depression, where getting outside is itself part of the work.
  • Anyone who finds an hour of eye contact harder than the topic.

It is not for everyone

A trail is a public place, and your confidentiality is maintained there exactly as it is in a room. Routes, timing and how conversation is handled when other people pass are chosen with that in mind, and the specifics are settled in the consult and the first online sessions rather than assumed.

Sessions are weather dependent and in central Texas that is not a formality. If the weather makes walking a bad idea, the session is rescheduled rather than pushed through. Online sessions remain the default for most of the work, with walking as part of it rather than all of it.

Walk sessions are for adults, 18 and over. The practice does not work with young children, and these sessions are not offered to anyone under 18.

With horses

Equine-assisted sessions run near Dripping Springs after the same consult and one to three online sessions, for an additional fee. Horses respond to what your nervous system is doing rather than what you intend, which makes them a direct teacher of presence. Equine work for therapists is separate and runs through the training side of the practice.

What is actually out there

Central Texas trails in season. Part of the point is that the view changes week to week while the conversation carries on.

Where the sessions happen

Shade, a fence line, somewhere to sit when walking stops being the point. Sessions move between all three, and nobody has to explain why they want to stop.

How it starts

  1. A free fifteen-minute consult. Say what is going on and whether being outside appeals or worries you.
  2. One to three online sessions. Enough for orientation, pacing and to know each other before the setting changes.
  3. Book a Friday and pay in advance. Advance payment holds the spot. There are no refunds for cancellations inside 48 hours.

Questions about walk and talk therapy

What is walk and talk therapy?

A therapy session held outdoors while walking, rather than seated in an office or on video. The clinical work is the same and the confidentiality obligations are the same; the setting changes the pressure of the conversation and gives the body something to do.

How much does a walk therapy session cost?

$240 to $370 per session depending on length, for roughly 75 minutes to two hours. It is paid in advance to hold the spot, with no refunds for cancellations inside 48 hours. Regular 50-minute online sessions with Reem are $240.

Can I start with a walk session?

No. Walk, movement and equine sessions begin after a free consult and one to three online sessions, so the pacing and the working relationship are established before the setting changes.

How is privacy handled outdoors?

Your confidentiality is maintained outdoors just as it is indoors. Because a trail is public, that is a planning question rather than an afterthought: route and timing, how conversation is handled when someone passes, and what you would want to do if you saw someone you know. All of it is agreed before the first walk.

Where do the walk sessions happen?

On trails in central Texas, on Fridays. The specific location is arranged with you, and the equine sessions are near Dripping Springs.

Is walk and talk therapy available for teenagers?

No. Trail walk, movement and equine sessions are for adults 18 and over. The practice sees adults and young adults, including college-age clients, for online therapy, and does not work with young children.

How to choose

Availability and fee decide it more often than specialty does. If you already know what you are bringing, the table above points at one or two people. If you do not, say what is going on in a few sentences through the contact page and you will be pointed at the right fit rather than left to guess.

What supervision means for you

An LPC Associate in Texas is fully qualified and licensed to practice, and is completing the 3,000 supervised hours the state requires before full licensure. Their work is reviewed every month by a Council-approved supervisor, which here means Reem.

In practice that means a second experienced clinician is thinking about your case alongside the person in the room. The licensure guide explains the requirement in full.

Note for the site build: add the client session fee and the session length once Reem confirms them. The $60 figure is the supervision rate for associates, not the client rate, and the two should not be conflated on a public page.

What a horse notices

Prey animals survive by reading intention and arousal faster and more accurately than we do. A horse will move away from someone who is saying all the right things while holding their breath, and settle next to someone who has genuinely arrived. It is not mystical. It is a very good sensor pointed at exactly the thing therapy usually has to infer from words.

That makes horses an unusually direct teacher of presence, and an unusually honest mirror for the gap between what you intend and what you are actually doing. People who have spent years being competent at therapy often meet something here they have been able to talk their way around indoors.

The horse is Blu. He is not a prop and he is not trained to perform anything therapeutic; he simply responds to whoever is standing in front of him, which is the entire point.

What happens in a session

  • Arriving, and noticing what your body does on the way in.
  • Being near the horse, without a task, longer than feels comfortable.
  • Simple ground work: approaching, leading, stopping, asking.
  • Talking about what just happened, which is where the therapy lives.

Why online sessions come first

One to three online sessions before the first equine session is not a formality. It establishes pacing, gives you a way to settle that you have already practiced, and means neither of us is meeting the other for the first time in a field. The same requirement applies to trail walk sessions.

Who it suits

People who talk more easily when something else is happening. People whose self-awareness is strong in words and thin in the body. People working on boundaries, because asking a thousand-pound animal to move is boundaries with the abstraction removed.

Who it does not

Anyone under 18, anyone with a horse allergy, and anyone currently in crisis, for whom stabilization online comes first. If you are frightened of horses, that is worth discussing rather than ruling yourself out: fear is workable material, but it should be chosen rather than endured.

How the methods work, in plain language

Reem's focus is IFS-informed EMDR: EMDR run with parts awareness, so the protective parts of you get consulted rather than overridden. It sits alongside two other approaches. Somatic Experiencing works with the nervous system directly, in small doses, to widen what you can tolerate. NARM works with the patterns that formed in childhood and how they still shape your present. Brainspotting comes in where it helps.

Start here

The four methods

NARM

The NeuroAffective Relational Model. Where a lifelong pattern was learned, how it was serving you, and whether it still is.

Somatic Experiencing

What the body is still holding, approached in doses small enough to integrate rather than flood.

EMDR

Finishing the processing of experiences stored raw, with stabilization first. EMDR certified, EMDRIA Approved Consultant.

IFS-informed EMDR

Where most of the work happens. For developmental trauma, and for EMDR that has stalled, flooded or gone nowhere.

Brainspotting and BASE-P come in where they help, and are not separate courses of treatment so much as alternate routes when the main ones will not settle.

How they fit together

They are not four separate treatments you pick between. In practice they interlock: NARM asks what pattern is running and where it was learned, Somatic Experiencing sets the pace your nervous system can hold, and IFS-informed EMDR does the processing once the first two have made room for it.

Which one leads on a given day depends on what you arrive with. A week of acute stress calls for stabilization. A recurring relational pattern calls for curiosity. A memory that keeps intruding calls for processing, once the parts holding it are on board.

You do not have to sort yourself into the right method before making contact. That is what the consult is for.

Questions about the methods

Which method will Reem use with me?

Whichever the week calls for. She is a NARM therapist, a Somatic Experiencing Practitioner and EMDR certified, so the approaches move with what you bring rather than being chosen in advance. NARM tracks the pattern, Somatic Experiencing sets the pacing, IFS-informed EMDR handles processing when there is room for it.

Do the methods get used in the same session?

Often, yes. They are not sequential modules. A single session can start with noticing what the body is doing, name the pattern that showed up, and end without processing anything at all if that is what the day holds.

Why not just do standard EMDR?

For a single discrete trauma with a stable nervous system, standard protocol often works well. When trauma is developmental and layered, parts of you have organized around keeping it away, and processing that skips those parts tends to flood, stall or stop working. Consulting them first is slower at the start and faster overall.

What is Brainspotting, and where does it fit?

An approach that uses fixed eye position to access where material is held, developed out of EMDR practice. Here it is an alternate route rather than a main one: useful when EMDR targeting will not settle, or when a client processes more easily without the back-and-forth of bilateral stimulation.

The spine of the developmental trauma work here

NARM therapy

NARM, the NeuroAffective Relational Model, is a therapy for developmental trauma: the patterns laid down early, before you had words or choices, that still shape how you meet your own life. It starts from curiosity rather than diagnosis, and it works with what the past installed rather than excavating the past itself. Reem Glasco, LPC-S, is a NARM therapist, and NARM is the spine of most of her work with developmental trauma. Sessions are 50 minutes at $240 self-pay, online anywhere in Texas, with Blue Cross Blue Shield accepted.

What NARM actually does

Every child adapts to the environment they are given. If closeness was unsafe, you learned distance. If your needs made things worse, you learned not to have them. If being competent earned the only reliable attention going, you learned to be useful. Those are not flaws. They are solutions that worked, and they kept working long after the conditions that required them had gone.

NARM calls these adaptive survival styles, and its interest is not in cataloguing them but in what they cost you today. The invitation is to notice how a pattern keeps you from being present in your own life, and to discover through felt sense which direction leads toward thriving rather than toward more of the same.

This is why NARM is less about the story than most therapies. The history matters, but understanding your history is famously compatible with nothing changing. What shifts things is working with the pattern as it shows up in the room, in the present tense.

It tends to fit when

  • The trouble is a lifelong pattern rather than a single event.
  • You understand your history intellectually and nothing has changed.
  • Self-criticism is doing most of the talking.
  • You disconnect from what you want before you have finished wanting it.
  • Other people's needs arrive clearly and your own arrive late or not at all.

How a NARM session feels

Slower than you expect, and more curious than sympathetic. The question is rarely what happened and more often what is happening right now as you say it: what your attention does, where it goes instead, what arrives in your body when you name something you want.

Agency is the quiet subject throughout. Developmental trauma teaches people that their own impulses are dangerous or irrelevant, and NARM keeps returning the choice to you, including the choice to not go there today.

What it is not

It is not catharsis, and it does not ask you to relive anything. It is also not advice. If you want a therapist who will tell you what to do about your mother, this is the wrong model and worth saying so early.

Questions about NARM

What is NARM therapy?

NARM is the NeuroAffective Relational Model, a therapy developed by Dr Laurence Heller for developmental trauma. It works with the adaptive survival patterns formed early in life and with how they shape the present, rather than with the events themselves. Its organizing question is where a pattern was learned, how it was serving you, and whether it still is.

What does NARM stand for?

The NeuroAffective Relational Model. Neuro for the nervous system, affective for emotion, relational because the patterns it works with formed in relationships and show up in them.

How is NARM different from regular talk therapy?

Conventional talk therapy tends to build an account of what happened. NARM is interested in what is happening now: how you relate to what you are saying, where your attention goes instead, and what your body does when you name something you want. Insight is a side effect rather than the goal.

Is NARM the same as somatic therapy?

No, though they overlap and are often used together. Somatic therapy works primarily through bodily sensation. NARM works with identity, agency and the adaptive patterns that organize them, using felt sense as one source of information among several.

How long does NARM therapy take?

Longer than single-incident work, because the target is capacity rather than a symptom. Patterns built over a childhood do not unwind in six sessions. The arc is reviewed together as the work goes rather than promised at the start.

Can I do NARM therapy online?

Yes, and it is the default here. NARM tracks your attention, your relationship to what you are saying and your felt sense, none of which require being in the same room. Both you and your therapist must be physically located in Texas during a session.

Working with the body, in doses

Somatic Experiencing

Somatic Experiencing, developed by Dr Peter Levine, treats trauma as something the body is still holding rather than a story the mind needs to retell. Sessions track physical sensation and the small movements a threat response never got to finish. Reem Glasco, LPC-S, is a Somatic Experiencing Practitioner (SEP). Sessions are 50 minutes at $240 self-pay, online anywhere in Texas, with Blue Cross Blue Shield accepted.

Why the body and not the story

When something overwhelming happens, the body prepares a response: fight, flee, brace, freeze. If the response cannot finish, because escape was impossible or you were too small or it simply went on too long, the preparation does not evaporate. It stays, as a chest that will not unclench, a jaw set at rest, a startle that fires at nothing.

That is why insight so often fails to move these symptoms. You can understand the origin of your bracing perfectly and still brace. Somatic Experiencing goes at the unfinished response directly.

Titration, the part that matters

The work is titrated: slow, and in doses. This is not caution for its own sake. A nervous system that gets flooded learns that attention to the body is dangerous, and then the next attempt is harder than the last. Done at a pace your system can integrate, the same work widens your window of tolerance instead of narrowing it.

It tends to fit when

  • Shock trauma is in the picture: an accident, an assault, a medical event.
  • You go numb, or flood, when you talk about hard things.
  • Anxiety lives in your chest and stomach more than in your thoughts.
  • Sleep does not restore you.
  • Talking about it has stopped helping.

What a session involves

Gentle attention to what is happening physically: temperature, pressure, breath, impulses to move. The first work is establishing a felt sense of safety, because nothing useful happens without it. From there you build the ability to notice a sensation, stay with it briefly, and come back out, which is the skill the whole method rests on.

You are not asked to narrate the trauma. Many people find they say less in SE than in the therapy they have done before, and that this is a relief rather than a loss.

On the evidence

Honest version: Somatic Experiencing has randomized controlled trials supporting it for PTSD symptoms and a wider body of observational work, and it does not yet have the decades of replication behind the cognitive-behavioral therapies. It is a reasonable, researched choice, not a proven superior one, and anyone selling it as either settled science or nonsense is overstating their case.

Questions about Somatic Experiencing

What is Somatic Experiencing?

Somatic Experiencing is a body-based trauma therapy developed by Dr Peter Levine. It treats a trauma response as something left unfinished in the nervous system rather than a problem of belief, so the work happens through physical sensation: what your body is doing, in small amounts, with regular returns to something steadier.

You are not asked to retell what happened. Sessions move in deliberately small pieces, and that pacing is the method rather than a courtesy.

What happens in a Somatic Experiencing session?

You are guided to notice what is happening in your body: sensation, breath, pressure, impulses to move. The therapist works first to establish a felt sense of safety, then helps you approach difficult material in small pieces and come back out again. You are not asked to retell the trauma.

What is titration in somatic therapy?

Breaking trauma work into pieces small enough that your system can process them without being overwhelmed or retraumatized. It is the central safeguard of the method, and it is why Somatic Experiencing usually feels slower than people expect.

Is Somatic Experiencing the same as somatic massage or bodywork?

No. Somatic Experiencing is psychotherapy and involves no touch in this practice, which works online. The word somatic means it attends to the body; it does not mean hands-on treatment.

How many Somatic Experiencing sessions will I need?

Shock trauma can shift in a handful. Chronic bracing laid down over years takes longer, because the goal is a wider window of tolerance rather than the removal of one symptom. It is reviewed together rather than fixed at the start.

Does Somatic Experiencing work over video?

Yes, and it is how this practice delivers it. The work tracks your own sensation rather than the room, so video is not the obstacle people expect. Both you and your therapist have to be physically located in Texas during a session.

What is the difference between Somatic Experiencing and EMDR?

EMDR reprocesses specific memories using dual attention. Somatic Experiencing works with the state of the nervous system and does not require a target memory at all. In this practice they are used together: Somatic Experiencing builds the capacity, EMDR does the processing once there is room for it.

EMDR, Eye Movement Desensitization and Reprocessing, helps the brain finish processing experiences it stored in raw form. What EMDR does

Some experiences get stored the way they arrived: raw, out of sequence, still carrying the body state that came with them. A sound, a smell or a tone of voice reaches that storage directly, and you are back in it before you have decided anything. EMDR gives the brain the conditions to file the material properly, so the memory stays and the hijack stops.

The dual attention task, following eye movements or taps while holding the material, is the part everyone has heard of. It is not hypnosis and it is not a trance. You stay awake, aware, and able to stop at any point.

Stabilization comes first

Reem's emphasis is the preparation phases: acute stress, ongoing stress, feeling overwhelmed, loss. Only with that footing does processing become useful rather than destabilizing. This is also the most common reason people arrive here saying EMDR did not work for them, and it is usually a preparation problem rather than a protocol failure.

It tends to fit when

  • Specific memories intrude, or certain triggers reliably hijack you.
  • You are in an ongoing stressful situation and need footing before insight.
  • Talking about it has stopped helping.
  • You want the charge out of something, not a better account of it.

On the controversy

Worth stating plainly, since it is the thing people read about. The outcomes are not in dispute: EMDR is recommended for PTSD by major bodies and trials consistently show it helps. The mechanism is. Dismantling studies that strip out the eye movements often find similar results, which suggests the bilateral stimulation may matter less than the structured exposure and reprocessing around it. It works, and the field does not fully agree on why.

Questions about EMDR

What is EMDR therapy?

EMDR stands for Eye Movement Desensitization and Reprocessing. You hold a difficult memory in mind while following a repeating left-right cue, usually eye movements, tapping or alternating sound. Attending to both at once appears to let the memory settle as something that happened rather than something still happening. The facts do not change. The charge on them does.

It is a structured therapy of eight phases rather than a technique used on its own, and most of the work here happens in the first two. In this practice EMDR is almost always IFS-informed, which means the preparation gets more attention than the standard protocol requires.

Can I do EMDR therapy online in Texas?

Yes, and it is the default here. Bilateral stimulation adapts to video using self-administered tapping or on-screen movement, and the preparation work is unaffected. Both you and your therapist must be physically located in Texas during the session.

What are the eight phases of EMDR?

History taking, preparation, assessment, desensitization, installation, body scan, closure and reevaluation. The first two are where this practice spends most of its effort, because insufficient preparation is the usual reason the later phases fail.

Does EMDR make you relive the trauma?

No. You hold the material in mind while attending to something else, which is the opposite of immersion, and the dual attention is what keeps one foot in the present. If you are flooding, the pacing is wrong and that is information rather than failure.

What is an EMDRIA Approved Consultant?

A clinician approved by the EMDR International Association to provide the consultation hours other therapists need for EMDR certification. It is a credential about teaching EMDR, not only practicing it, and it requires certification plus substantial supervised consultation experience.

Is EMDR covered by insurance?

Insurers reimburse by session code rather than by method, so an EMDR session bills as individual psychotherapy. Blue Cross Blue Shield is accepted here; sessions under any other plan are self-pay at $240 for 50 minutes.

How much does EMDR therapy cost?

The same as any other session here: $240 for 50 minutes, self-pay, with Blue Cross Blue Shield accepted. EMDR is not billed as a separate or premium service and there is no package to buy up front. The practice's LPC Associates see clients at lower fees, including on a sliding scale. Everything is listed on the FAQ.

Therapists seeking EMDRIA-approved consultation hours rather than therapy pay $185 an hour, which is a different arrangement.

Who should not do EMDR?

Nobody is ruled out by diagnosis, but timing matters. Active crisis, an unstable living situation, or having no reliable way to settle yourself afterward are all reasons to build footing first rather than start processing. That judgment is part of what the consult and the preparation phases are for.

This practice does not provide emergency care. If you are in immediate danger, call 911. For a mental health crisis, call or text 988 for the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline.

Where most of the work happens

IFS-informed EMDR

Standard EMDR asks you to hold a memory and let the processing run. For people with developmental trauma that instruction often meets an internal objection: a part of you that has spent years keeping the material at a distance, and has good reasons. IFS-informed EMDR treats that objection as information rather than resistance. Processing starts when the protective parts agree to it, not when the protocol says it is time. This is the focus of Reem Glasco's clinical work, and the reason most people arrive here. Sessions are 50 minutes at $240 self-pay, online across Texas, with Blue Cross Blue Shield accepted.

Why standard EMDR stalls

If the trauma is a single event and your nervous system is otherwise stable, standard protocol often works well and quickly. If the trauma is developmental, something else is true: parts of you organized around keeping that material away, and they did it for years, competently, because at the time it was the only thing keeping you functional.

Ask those parts to stand aside for a protocol and they will do what they have always done. The processing floods, or it flatlines, or you find yourself unable to bring the target to mind at all. From the outside it looks like EMDR not working. From the inside it is a protector doing its job.

What changes with parts work

Internal Family Systems gives us language for that. Rather than pushing past the protector, we get to know it. What is it afraid will happen if you go near this? What does it need in place first? What has it been carrying, and for how long?

Reem's emphasis is phases one and two, history-taking and preparation, because that is where stalled EMDR actually stalls. Build enough stability and enough internal agreement there, and the later phases stop being a fight.

What this looks like in session

  • Naming the parts in the room: the one that wants to heal, the one that wants to leave, the one that thinks this is self-indulgent.
  • Unblending, so you can look at a part rather than speak as it.
  • Asking permission from protectors before any target gets processed.
  • Resourcing and stabilization that a protective part actually trusts.
  • Slowing or pausing processing when a part objects, and treating that objection as information rather than resistance.

It tends to fit when

  • EMDR has been tried before and went nowhere, or went badly.
  • You flood, dissociate or go blank when you approach the material.
  • Part of you wants this and part of you really does not.
  • The trauma is developmental and layered rather than a single event.

Reem completed steps one through three of IFS-informed EMDR training in 2025, is EMDR certified and an EMDRIA Approved Consultant, and consults with other therapists on exactly this problem.

Questions about IFS-informed EMDR

What is Internal Family Systems?

A model that treats the mind as made up of parts, each with its own job and its own fears, around a core self that is not a part. Protective parts manage pain; exiled parts carry it. The work is relational: you get to know a part rather than overriding it.

Is this the same as full IFS therapy?

No. This is EMDR practiced with IFS awareness, not IFS as a standalone treatment. The parts work is in service of making EMDR usable for developmental trauma, particularly in the preparation phases.

My EMDR flooded me last time. Will that happen again?

It is the specific thing this approach exists to prevent. Flooding usually means processing started before the parts holding the material had agreed to it, or before there was enough resourcing for them to trust. Both are preparation problems, and preparation is where the emphasis sits here.

How is this different from just going slower?

Pace helps, but the obstacle is not usually speed. A protector that believes something catastrophic follows from touching this material will object at any speed. What changes things is finding out what it is protecting and what it needs, which is a different conversation rather than a slower one.

Do I have to believe in parts for this to work?

No. Parts language is a working model, not a metaphysics. Plenty of people use it as a convenient way of describing conflicting impulses they already recognize, and the work proceeds the same either way.

A gentle self-care workbook

Effort-less Self-Care

7 Easy Steps to Calm and Connection

Slow down and build a relationship with your body, your breath and your inner self. There is nothing here to fix. Notice yourself, be kind to yourself, stay curious. Healing begins when you learn to listen. Written by Reem Glasco, LPC-S, the workbook sets out seven short steps, each paired with watercolor imagery and journal prompts, to be used daily or whenever you need to reset. The workbook and the journal are one volume: you read a step, then write on the pages that follow it. It costs $14.95.

Try the seven steps Find it on Barnes & Noble (opens in a new tab)

The value of pause

“You start the healing process when you learn to listen to your body.”

The workbook shows you how to ground yourself in the present moment, one simple step at a time. Use the seven steps as a daily or weekly practice whenever you need to reset. Getting stuck is fine. Your body resisting is part of the journey. Always remember to breathe.

The practice

Seven easy steps to calm and connection

Each step is a small, gentle invitation, paired in the book with soft watercolor imagery and journal prompts to guide your own exploration.

Step 1

Find Your Comfortable Space

“Comfort is where healing begins.”

Pause and find a place, indoors or outdoors, that invites calm. Notice how it feels in your body.

Step 2

Face the Light

“Let the sun guide you.”

Face the morning sun, east, a symbol of new beginnings. Picture the light warming your face.

Step 3

Return to Your Heart

“Come home to your breath.”

Place your hand on your chest and feel your breath. Do not change it, just notice it.

Step 4

Breathe in Peace, Breathe out Stress

“Breathe in fresh air; breathe out stress.”

Inhale: I am breathing in fresh air. Exhale: I am breathing out stress. Repeat softly three times.

Step 5

Pause and Feel

“Your body speaks. Listen.”

Scan from head to toe. Observe where you feel tension, pressure or pain, and what your body is telling you.

Step 6

Gently Name What You Feel

“Name it to know it.”

Label the emotion without judgment. Ask what it is trying to tell you, and what sits underneath the story.

Step 7

Ground Yourself Through Your Senses

“Your senses ground you in the now.”

Notice what you see, hear, smell, taste and touch. Sit with any positive shift for at least seventeen seconds.

About the author

Guiding you gently back to yourself

Reem Glasco is a Licensed Professional Counselor Supervisor in Texas who believes self-care should not be one more thing to get right. Her approach is spacious and kind: meet your nervous system where it is, understand what your body is signalling, and learn to pause even in the middle of chaos.

Effort-less Self-Care distils that philosophy into seven approachable steps, so that over time you reset more quickly, settle more deeply, and feel more grounded.

The same lineage runs through her clinical work: NARM, Somatic Experiencing and IFS-informed EMDR, all of which begin with sensation rather than analysis. More about Reem.

Step 1 of 7

Find Your Comfortable Space

“Comfort is where healing begins.”

Take a moment to pause and find a place, indoors or outdoors, that inspires a sense of calm and comfort. You may even hold a small piece of nature: a stone, a leaf, a shell. Notice how you feel, but there is no need to change anything.

Step 2 of 7

Face the Light

“Let the sun guide you.”

When sitting, face the morning sun, east. This is not just a direction; it stands for new beginnings. Picture the light warming your face, and feel what arises.

Step 3 of 7

Return to Your Heart

“Come home to your breath.”

Place your hand on your chest and feel your breath. Do not change it, just notice it. Sit like this for about thirty seconds.

Where do my answers go?

Nowhere. They are saved in your browser's local storage on this device and never transmitted. Reem cannot see them, this site has no analytics, and there is no account to create. The trade-off is that clearing your browsing data deletes them.

Do I have to answer every prompt?

How often should I do this?

Reem Glasco, LPC-S

Reem Glasco is a Licensed Professional Counselor Supervisor in Texas, license 66562, and has held supervisor status since 2009 with over fifteen years of clinical experience. She is a NARM therapist, a Somatic Experiencing Practitioner (SEP), EMDR certified and an EMDRIA Approved Consultant. She was a Clinical Partner at Capital Area Counseling from 2021 to 2025 and practices from Cedar Park, Texas, working online statewide.

How I work

My NARM approach is an invitation to be curious about your patterns, and about how they keep you from being present in your own life. Where did I learn this? How was it serving me? How does being present give me a choice about which path leads to thriving?

My EMDR work is IFS-informed, which means the protective parts of you get consulted before anything gets processed, and my emphasis is on phases one and two where that agreement is built. It is weighted toward stabilization: acute stress, ongoing stress, overwhelm, loss. My Somatic Experiencing approach meets shock trauma in a titrated way, slow and gentle, building your window of tolerance rather than testing it.

I teach effortless self care through walk and mindful therapy, and I run mindful trail retreats for interns, associates and therapists, where we explore being present and what gets in the way of it.

I am also an LPC supervisor. Supervision is online, and I offer mindful retreats for associate therapists to expand their personal and professional awareness in the field.

You can also find me on Psychology Today.

The work itself

What kind of therapy does Reem practice?

NARM for the patterns formed early in life, Somatic Experiencing for what the nervous system is still holding, and EMDR for specific traumatic material once there is enough stability. IFS-informed and Brainspotting elements are used where parts of a person disagree about the work.

Understanding the methods

What is somatic therapy?

Somatic therapy is any approach that works with the body's sensations and responses rather than with thoughts alone. The working assumption is that stress and trauma leave the nervous system holding an unfinished response, and that noticing that response directly, in small doses, does what analyzing it cannot. In practice a session tracks sensation, breath, posture and the small movements a threat response never completed. Somatic Experiencing, developed by Dr Peter Levine, is the somatic method used here.

Is EMDR a somatic therapy?

Partly. EMDR is not usually classed as a somatic therapy, because its core mechanism is memory reprocessing rather than body tracking. But it attends closely to where a memory sits in the body and it pairs naturally with somatic work, which is why both are used in this practice rather than one or the other.

Is somatic therapy evidence based?

The evidence base is real but smaller than for CBT or EMDR. Somatic Experiencing has randomised controlled trials supporting it for PTSD symptoms, and a wider body of observational work; it does not yet have the decades of replication that the cognitive-behavioral therapies have. Anyone who tells you it is either proven beyond question or pure invention is overstating their case.

Is somatic therapy covered by insurance?

Insurers reimburse psychotherapy sessions by billing code rather than by method, so a somatic session is billed as individual psychotherapy like any other. Blue Cross Blue Shield is accepted here. Under other plans sessions are self-pay at $240 for 50 minutes, and you may be able to claim out-of-network reimbursement.

Why is EMDR so controversial?

The outcomes are not what is disputed. EMDR is recommended for PTSD by the World Health Organization and the American Psychological Association, and trials consistently show it helps. What is disputed is the mechanism: dismantling studies that strip out the eye movements often find similar results, which suggests the bilateral stimulation may matter less than the structured exposure and reprocessing around it. So the honest summary is that it works and the field does not fully agree on why.

Is EMDR hypnosis?

No. You stay awake, aware and in control throughout, you can stop at any point, and you remember the session afterwards. Nobody is put into a trance or given suggestions. The eye movements or taps are a dual-attention task, not an induction.

How long does EMDR therapy take?

For a single recent incident, often six to twelve sessions. For developmental trauma laid down over years it is longer, because most of the work is in preparation and stabilization rather than in processing. Reem's emphasis is deliberately on phases one and two, since that is where stalled EMDR usually stalls.

Can EMDR be done virtually?

Yes, and it is the default here. Bilateral stimulation adapts to video using self-administered tapping or on-screen movement, and the preparation and resourcing work is unaffected. Both you and your therapist must be physically located in Texas during the session.

Complex PTSD

What are the 17 symptoms of complex PTSD?

There is no official list of 17. That number comes from the DSM-IV criteria for PTSD, which counted 17 symptoms across re-experiencing, avoidance and arousal, and it has been recycled online as though it described complex PTSD. It does not. Complex PTSD is defined in the ICD-11 as the three PTSD clusters plus three further disturbances: difficulty regulating emotion, a persistently negative view of yourself, and difficulty sustaining relationships and feeling close to people. A checklist is not a diagnosis, and a recognisable pattern is worth bringing to an assessment rather than settling in your own head.

What is the difference between PTSD and complex PTSD?

PTSD usually follows an identifiable event or a small number of them. Complex PTSD follows prolonged, repeated exposure that was hard or impossible to escape, often early and often relational. The extra ground it covers is how you relate to yourself and to other people, not just how you respond to reminders of what happened.

Is complex PTSD in the DSM-5?

No. The DSM-5 recognizes PTSD, including a dissociative subtype, but not complex PTSD as a separate diagnosis. The ICD-11, published by the World Health Organization, does. That difference matters mostly for paperwork: in the United States the clinical record and any insurance claim will usually say PTSD.

Does EMDR work for complex PTSD?

It can, with the preparation phases taken seriously. Applied straight to developmental trauma without that groundwork, standard EMDR often floods or flatlines, which is the most common reason people arrive here saying EMDR did not work for them. The IFS-informed version addresses exactly that.

How many EMDR sessions for complex PTSD?

More than the six to twelve typical of single-incident work, and the honest answer is that it depends on how much stabilization is needed first. Rather than committing to a number at the start, the arc is reviewed together as the work goes.

Is complex PTSD a disability?

It can be, depending on how much it limits daily functioning rather than on the label itself. Because complex PTSD is not a separate DSM-5 diagnosis, claims in the United States are generally filed under PTSD. Whether a particular claim succeeds is a question for a treating clinician and someone who handles disability claims, not for a website.

For therapists

How many supervised hours do I need for a Texas LPC?

3,000 clock-hours under a Council-approved supervisor, at least 1,500 of them direct client counseling contact, over no fewer than 18 months, with a minimum of four supervision hours a month and no more than half of your total supervision hours in a group. The licensure guide on this site works through all of it, including the 60-month expiry on your Associate license.

Do you run retreats or training for therapists?

Yes. An annual mindful trail retreat for interns, associates and licensed therapists, equine-assisted sessions and training near Dripping Springs, and periodic ethics continuing education for Texas LPCs. Associates in supervision with Reem are included in the annual retreat.

Are you accepting LPC Associates for supervision?

One supervision spot opens in fall 2026 and one in spring 2027. Supervision is $425 a month for four individual hours and one group hour, online and statewide in Texas. Applications start with a free 30-minute consult.

Can my agency contract supervision for a short period?

Yes. Three-month contracts are available for associates working within an agency or group practice at $500 a month.

Can you be my EMDR consultant?

Reem is an EMDRIA Approved Consultant. Individual consultation is $185 an hour online, focused on IFS-informed EMDR for phases one and two, and it is free for her own LPC associates.

Do you offer ethics CEUs?

Ethics continuing education for Texas LPCs is offered periodically. Email the practice to ask about the next session.

Safety

What if I am in crisis right now?

This practice does not provide emergency care. Call 911 if you are in immediate danger, or call or text 988 for the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline. Reach out here once you are safe and we can talk about ongoing support.
