Notes · March 2020

How to set healthy boundaries

A healthy relationship leaves both people room to be themselves and keep their integrity intact. Plenty of people end up alongside someone who treats their limits as negotiable and their own needs as the ones that matter. If holding a boundary feels almost impossible, that is usually learned rather than innate: in a chaotic or insecure household, limits get overridden often enough that you stop setting them.

Five steps

  1. Identify your limits. You cannot hold a boundary you have not worked out. Before anything is said to anyone, get clear on what you will and will not accept, what reliably drains or upsets you, and what actually makes you feel good. Vagueness here is what turns a boundary into a negotiation later.
  2. Do not be shy about saying it. People come from different families and read situations differently. An implied boundary is often simply not perceived, and the other person is not necessarily ignoring you so much as missing it entirely. Say it plainly, directly and out loud. This is uncomfortable and it is still the shortest route.
  3. Pay attention to your feelings. Your own reaction is the instrument. Notice how you feel during and after an interaction, in a journal if that helps. Resentment and anger are the reliable signals that a limit was crossed. When they turn up, restate the boundary. If it keeps being disregarded after that, withdrawing from the interaction is a legitimate response rather than a failure.
  4. Make self-care a priority. Putting your own needs first feels wrong to anyone who has spent years meeting everyone else's, and the discomfort is not evidence that you are doing something selfish. Give yourself permission to have needs and to meet them. Boundaries held out of obligation collapse; boundaries held because you believe you are allowed to have them do not.
  5. Speak with someone. If boundaries keep collapsing, the obstacle is usually not technique. It is a thin sense of your own worth, and that is hard to argue yourself out of alone. A therapist can trace where those feelings came from and work on the thinking and the behavior attached to them.

Why this is often harder than it sounds

If your limits were routinely overridden early on, the nervous system learned something practical: asserting a need costs more than absorbing the harm. That lesson does not expire on its own, and it does not respond to being told it is irrational.

This is the territory NARM works in, and it is why boundary trouble so often turns out to be developmental trauma wearing a practical disguise.

If you want to work on this, a consult is free and fifteen minutes.

Request a consult Trauma therapy here

Common questions about boundaries

Why do I feel guilty every time I set a boundary?

Because guilt is what you were trained to feel. If having needs once made things worse at home, the alarm still fires when you have one, regardless of what you now believe. The guilt is a signal about your history rather than a verdict on your behavior.

What if someone keeps ignoring my boundary?

Restate it once, plainly. If it is still disregarded after that, the remaining option is to change your own exposure rather than their behavior, which may mean less contact or a different kind of contact. That is a boundary too.

Is a boundary the same thing as an ultimatum?

No. An ultimatum tries to control what the other person does. A boundary states what you will do, and it works even if they never change. If you find yourself issuing conditions and waiting to see whether they comply, that is something else.

Home / Client Forms

Client forms

New clients complete a short set of forms before the first session, so the hour is spent on you rather than on paperwork. There are five: an intake, a client information sheet, the Limits of Confidentiality notice, your Good Faith Estimate, and a release of information you only need if records are being shared with someone else.

Request the forms See fees first

The forms

Client Intake
History, what brings you, and what you want from the work. Sent to you by email before your first session.
Client Information
Contact details, emergency contact, and payment information. Sent to you by email before your first session.
Limits of Confidentiality
What stays in the room and the narrow situations where it cannot. Required. Sent to you by email before your first session.
Good Faith Estimate
Your written cost estimate under the No Surprises Act. Required for self-pay clients. Sent to you by email before your first session.
Authorization for Release of Information
Only if you want records shared with a doctor, school or another clinician. Sent to you by email before your first session.

Complete them before your first session and the work starts in the first ten minutes rather than the last ten. If anything on them is unclear or uncomfortable to answer in writing, leave it and raise it in the room instead.

Two of these are not optional

Limits of Confidentiality

Therapy is confidential, and there are a small number of situations where Texas law requires a counselor to act anyway: a serious threat to your life or someone else's, and suspected abuse or neglect of a child, an elderly person or a person with a disability. The notice sets out exactly what those are. It is better read before you need it than after.

Good Faith Estimate

Under the federal No Surprises Act, anyone not billing through insurance has the right to a written estimate of what their care will cost, given before treatment starts. Yours covers the expected number of sessions and the fee for each. If the final bill ends up $400 or more above the estimate, you can dispute it.

Blue Cross Blue Shield clients are billed through insurance rather than self-pay, so the estimate works differently; ask in the consult. Fees and insurance in full.

Before you fill anything in

  • You do not need the forms to book a consult. The consult is free and commits you to nothing.
  • Seeing one of the associates instead? Each associate runs their own paperwork, so ask them directly.
  • Send completed forms the way you were told to send them. Email is not a secure channel for clinical detail.

Privacy

The practice's privacy policy explains how your information is stored, who can see it and how long it is kept. Ask for a copy at any point.

You can ask for your records at any time. Records are provided electronically within 15 business days of a written request, under the Texas Medical Records Privacy Act.

Questions about the paperwork

What forms do I need before my first therapy session?

Five: a client intake, a client information sheet, the Limits of Confidentiality notice, a Good Faith Estimate, and an authorization for release of information if records need to go to another provider. They take about fifteen minutes in total.

What is a Good Faith Estimate and do I get one?

It is a written estimate of what your care will cost, which the federal No Surprises Act entitles you to before treatment begins if you are not billing through insurance. It states the expected number of sessions and the fee for each, and if the final bill comes in $400 or more above it you have the right to dispute the charge.

Do I have to complete the forms before booking a consult?

No. The free consult comes first and needs nothing from you but a few sentences about what is going on. Paperwork only matters once you have decided to start.

Can I email the completed forms back?

Send them by whatever route you were given when the forms were sent. Ordinary email is not a secure channel for clinical information, which is why intake usually runs through a client portal instead.

Questions about booking and payment

How do I book a therapy session?

Existing clients book through the client portal. If you have not started yet, request a free 15-minute consult first; the portal invitation follows once you decide to go ahead. Clients of the practice's associates book directly with their associate.

How do I pay for a session?

By major credit card inside the client portal. Blue Cross Blue Shield is accepted and billed through insurance; sessions under any other plan are self-pay at $240 for 50 minutes. In-person walk therapy is paid in advance.

What happens if I cancel?

Telehealth appointments canceled at least 24 hours ahead cost nothing. Inside 24 hours an $85 fee may apply. Walk therapy is paid in advance and is not refunded for cancellations inside 48 hours.

Do I have to be in Texas for a telehealth session?

Yes. A Texas license allows a counselor to treat clients located in Texas, so both you and your therapist have to be physically in the state at the time of the session. Tell your therapist in advance if you are traveling, so the appointment can be moved rather than canceled.

Can I use the portal to reach my therapist between sessions?

For scheduling and admin, yes. It is not a crisis channel and messages are not monitored around the clock. If you are in immediate danger, call 911; for a mental health crisis, call or text 988.
